label: Full disk vs partition vs volume vs file vs database vs record encryption

mentor.diagnosis: You chose by how much the option encrypts rather than by what threat the stem describes. Each level protects against a different moment, and the broadest is not the strongest.
contrast: The device being stolen or lost while powered off
Anyone who is logged in: once booted, everything is transparent
The same, scoped to part of the disk
The same blind spot, plus whatever sits outside the protected volume
Access to one file by someone who can otherwise read the disk
Nothing, if the key is available to the same account
Theft of the database files or backups
A legitimate query: the database decrypts for authorised sessions
Exposure of specific sensitive fields even to database users
Fields you did not encrypt, and anyone with the key
Anything at either end, where it is plaintext
mentor.rule: Full disk protects a powered-off device. Record-level protects a field from people who can legitimately read the database. If the stem has an authorised user misusing access, disk encryption is never the answer.
mentor.tell: A lost laptop points to full disk. A DBA who should not see card numbers points to record or column level. A sniffed network points to transport.
mentor.trap: Full disk encryption is the most familiar answer and does nothing once the machine is running and unlocked, which is the state it spends almost all its life in.

label: Key exchange, key length, key escrow and the key management system

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the key as a detail of the algorithm. Most real cryptographic failures are key management failures: how the key got there, how long it is, and who else holds a copy.
contrast: Agreeing a shared secret over an untrusted channel, as with Diffie-Hellman
Sending the key alongside the ciphertext
The work an attacker must do to brute force
Comparing lengths across algorithm families as if they were equivalent
Using a primitive suited to the job and not deprecated
Choosing by familiarity: DES, MD5, SHA-1 still get picked
A third party holding a copy so data is recoverable
The copy is a second place to steal the key from
Generation, distribution, rotation, revocation and destruction
Keys living in source code and configuration files
mentor.rule: Key lengths compare only inside an algorithm family. A 256-bit symmetric key and a 2048-bit RSA key are roughly comparable in strength, which is why the numbers look so different.
mentor.tell: A stem about two parties with no prior contact establishing a shared secret, or about recovering data when an employee leaves.
mentor.trap: Escrow sounds like a weakness and is a deliberate trade: it is how an organisation reads its own encrypted data after someone departs. The exam wants you to know the trade-off exists, not to reject it.

label: TPM vs HSM vs secure enclave vs key management system

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on the word hardware. These differ by where they live, what they are for, and whether they serve one machine or many.
contrast: Root of trust for that device: measured boot, sealed keys
Full disk encryption key that only releases if boot state is unchanged
A dedicated appliance or card serving many systems
High-assurance key generation, storage and operations
A certificate authority's private key; payment processing
An isolated region of the main processor
Protecting keys and operations from the OS itself
Lifecycle: generation, rotation, revocation, destruction, policy
Managing thousands of keys across an estate
mentor.rule: A TPM anchors one machine. An HSM serves many and is built to be tamper-evident and certified. An enclave protects against the operating system on the same chip. A KMS manages the lifecycle, usually backed by one of the others.
mentor.tell: A stem about a key that must never leave hardware, or about disk encryption keys tied to a machine's boot state.
mentor.trap: A TPM is not an HSM. It is cheap, soldered down, and scoped to its own host. Proposing a TPM to protect a CA's signing key is the classic wrong answer.

label: Self-signed vs third-party vs wildcard certificates, and the CSR

mentor.diagnosis: You judged certificates by the encryption they enable. All of these encrypt identically. What differs is who vouches for the identity, and for how many names.
contrast: Internal systems where you distribute the trust yourself
Many subdomains at one level, such as *.example.com
mentor.rule: A CSR is generated on the system that will hold the private key, and the private key never leaves it. You send the CSR, you receive a signed certificate, and only the public half ever travels.
mentor.tell: Browser warnings on an internal site point to self-signed. A need to cover many subdomains points to wildcard. A key that was emailed anywhere points to a compromised process.
mentor.trap: A wildcard certificate covers one level only: *.example.com does not cover a.b.example.com. It also means one compromised private key exposes every host using it, which is why spreading a wildcard across many servers is a trade rather than a convenience.

label: Steganography vs tokenisation vs data masking vs hashing

mentor.diagnosis: You grouped these as 'ways of hiding data' and stopped there. They differ on whether the original can come back and who is meant to be fooled.
contrast: Yes, by whoever knows it is there
That any message exists at all
Yes, via a separate vault mapping
The real value in the system holding it
Card numbers that must still support refunds
Part or all of the value from the viewer
Showing only the last four digits to support staff
The content from anyone without the key
mentor.rule: Ask whether the original value needs to come back, and to whom. Hashing is the only one of these that is one way. Steganography is the only one hiding the existence of the message rather than its content.
mentor.tell: A stem about data that must remain usable for a business process while not being present in its real form.
mentor.trap: Steganography is often misremembered as a form of encryption. It provides no confidentiality: find the payload and you have it. Its property is concealment, which is why it appears in exfiltration scenarios rather than protection ones.

label: What a blockchain and an open public ledger actually provide

mentor.diagnosis: You assumed a blockchain provides confidentiality. It is built from hashing and digital signatures, and what it delivers is integrity and a verifiable shared history, not secrecy.
contrast: Does a public blockchain provide it
Each block commits to the previous one by hash, so altering history breaks every block after it
Entries are signed by the key that authorised them
An open public ledger is readable by anyone, which is what open means
Pseudonymous at best; addresses are persistent and linkable
mentor.rule: A blockchain is a tamper-evident append-only log maintained by people who do not trust each other. If the requirement is secrecy, it is the wrong tool.
mentor.tell: A scenario needing a shared record several parties can verify without a central authority.
mentor.trap: Immutable is shorthand, not a law of physics. The record is tamper-evident because changing it would be obvious to everyone holding a copy, not because the bytes cannot be edited.
